utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I remind you, Mrs. Cenic, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Cenic. Mrs. Cenic, did the -- after the work that you already described to the Trial Chamber upon your arrival at Pale, did the nature of your work subsequently change?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please clarify what exactly you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you described the sort of work you were doing at the Kikinda building in the, at least the first period after your arrival in Pale in July 1992 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seemed to be a technical problem but I think Judge Canivell will read the question and hear the answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I probably ought to start again just in case the witness needs it from the beginning, Your Honour, because she was asking for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, you described to the Trial Chamber the other day the sort of work you were doing at the Kikinda building, in at least the first period after your arrival in Pale in July 1992. And what I'm asking is whether the nature of your work changed at any subsequent point.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, afterwards, I worked for the Ministry of Information, if we are talking about 1992, and it was just for a brief period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I am talking about the short term of 1992, Mrs. Cenic, for clarification.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next, when everyone moved over to this other location, Mali Dom, I was with the National Assembly and my duty was to prepare for Mr. Krajisnik whatever was available from the press, whatever we were able to receive, and to make brief overviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, first of all, can you date, as best you can, the move over to the other location at Mali Dom?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in October, but I can't be certain. What I'm saying is to the best of my recollection. I believe it was October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the work that you did in relation to press materials and the making of brief overviews, did that include work on both Serbian language publications and English publications?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, we could not get hold of any foreign press. Perhaps only to the extent that foreign journalists and visitors brought along. As for any regular receipt of foreign press, that was quite impossible. We didn't have that. The press materials we did receive, whether through bus drivers who took them along or otherwise, consisted of the press from Serbia, some of our media, and sometimes we received the press materials from Sarajevo, whenever anyone from UNPROFOR arrived or the liaison officer for UNPROFOR, whenever he was able to bring along something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, from when you arrived in Pale in July 1992, as you've described, through to first of all when you moved to Mali Dom -- Mali Dom, so talking about before you moved to Mali Dom, did you personally attend any high-level political meetings of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware of such meetings taking place?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such meetings of any sort or of any level were, of course, held. Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Djeric, and commissioners for certain regions also came by.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a particular location where such meetings were generally held?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really mention any special occasions here, just as I can't tell you whether these meetings were of a formal or consultative nature, because I didn't attend the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware at any time of there being meetings of a body known as the Expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the Presidency, and there were broader meetings that Dr. Karadzic most often called brainstorming. I'm mentioning this term that he used because we tended to use this term "mozganje," brainstorming, later on, since Dr. Karadzic used to invite quite a few people for these discussions or consultations, and Professor Koljevic many years later used to joke about it, because these meetings were very frequently held in the evenings, which he, as a person, did not like because it simply did not suit his biorhythm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the joke, then?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of us used to call the meetings of this type Karadzic's brainstorming, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- did you ever hear or were you aware of any meetings that were called meetings of the Expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those of us who were members of the staff - and I say this with full responsibility - never called it Expanded Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware of any such body that was called the Expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For us, such a body did not exist. We knew of meetings that were most often convened by Dr. Karadzic, and one never knew for sure who it was that he was going to invite to the meeting. It was, of course, certain that Professor Koljevic would be invited, if he was there, and Mrs. Plavsic, if she was at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you personally, during the time when you were at Kikinda and before you went to Mali Dom, have any communication with Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How -- can you say how frequently you had telephone contact with him?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when Ratko Mladic - General Mladic - called, and if I was there to answer the phone, I know for a fact that it was him who called us more than me placing a call to him, as far as I remember. I called General Milovanovic most frequently, because it had to do with humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When General Mladic rang, were there particular people that he generally or frequently wished to speak to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic normally asked for Dr. Karadzic, and if Dr. Karadzic wasn't there, then, in his military tone, he would ask for a very brief message - always a very brief message - to be relayed to him. He always asked that Dr. Karadzic phone him back, normally as a matter of urgency, and along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During that period when you were at Kikinda, did you at any time actually see General Mladic in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can't really recall any instances whilst we were at Kikinda that I myself had occasion to see him, because he didn't go to the office where I was -- where I had my desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When Mr. Krajisnik was on the telephone in his office while you were working there, were you in a position to hear his conversation?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often I did because the telephone was in that office. Exceptionally, I'd leave the office because it wasn't really appropriate for me to be sitting at a desk with him behind my back, talking on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there occasions, then, when you did overhear his conversation?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Rare or quite often or --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Krajisnik discussing military strategy on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Krajisnik giving any sort of orders or instructions apparently to anybody connected with the military over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you please clarify, what instructions are you referring to? What sort of instructions do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, first of all, did you ever hear Mr. Krajisnik giving any sort of orders or instructions apparently to anybody military over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the instructions which would take the form of requests or discussions also came from me, when they had to do with humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Krajisnik giving any sort of orders or instructions to any police force over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek clarification of the last answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Cenic, the question was whether you ever did hear Mr. Krajisnik giving any sort of orders or instructions apparently to anybody military over the telephone. Your answer was: "At that time, the instructions which would take the form of request or discussions also came from me, when they had to do with humanitarian convoys."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik had, on several occasions, talked about humanitarian convoys which were on their way to Sarajevo, and which the army was to allow safe passage for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And these -- so I do understand that what you said, the instructions which would take the form of requests or discussions, were also instructions or requests and discussion of the military but, you say, on the subject of humanitarian convoys, and you say "they also came from me." Does that mean that you passed these messages for Mr. Krajisnik? It's not entirely clear to me what you meant by "also came from me."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Back then, Your Honour, humanitarian convoys were always a problem, and ensuring their safe passage too. In view of the fact that in a certain way I was able to persuade both General Mladic and General Milovanovic about the necessity to take immediate action, it was felt -- or rather, as Mr. Karadzic himself put it, I spoke their language, as it were, and that is why it was in a way left to me. Ceca, which is my nickname, they would say, "You will best explain this to them." Another explanation of this is that initially we had conflicts or, rather, I came into conflict with General Mladic and General Milovanovic, because I did not allow anyone to address me in such a tone of voice. I made it quite clear that they may as well be generals but not even my father addressed me in that tone. As a result of this, I seemed to have gained the respect of both General Mladic and General Milovanovic and we no longer had any communication problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if they would disagree, I take it that you would send with a message, try to convince General Mladic to let a convoy through, and if finally he said, no, for military purposes, I'd rather not at this moment have this convoy in this area, what would then happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then General Mladic or General Milovanovic - this in fact happened in one instance, what you just described - they asked that they be sent any sort of document, anything in writing, to that effect. And the document would normally be a letter from Mr. Karadzic containing information about the items transported in the convoy, whether these were medicines, foodstuffs, or something else, and the escorts to the convoy. It was my duty to convey this to them, and then the service of Mr. Karadzic was supposed to react. And when I say his service, I meant Dr. Karadzic and his secretary. However, sometimes or, rather, quite frequently, all of this would be a matter of urgency, requiring immediate action, and convoys had to be allowed passage basically just on the basis of a verbal request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the question started with Mr. Krajisnik, whether he ever gave any orders or instructions. Then in your answer you moved to Mr. Karadzic, and you gave an example which is not entirely clear to me yet. But let's perhaps first stick with your answer, your example you gave. I think you said that General Mladic wanted to have some kind of a paper. Paper from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received a piece of paper, an announcement of some sort. Sometimes the notice was short, but the convoy that was supposed to arrive would be announced, and General Mladic, and particularly Milovanovic, asked instructions in writing; a piece of paper, any sort of writing. They did not want this to be only a verbal announcement. When I mentioned Mr. Krajisnik and even myself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment. You said they -- you received a piece of paper, announcement, and then you said General Mladic, and particularly Milovanovic, asked instructions in writing. Who would give those instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that then -- you're talking about a piece of paper which is an announcement. Was that the same as the instructions or were the instructions accompanying or related in any way to the announcement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic would sign accompanying letters at the time, and together with his letter, there would also be a piece of paper announcing the convoy that was arriving. Different organisations were involved in the sending of humanitarian aid or other things, so that every organisation enclosed a piece of paper in their turn. There were a number of charity organisations, international ones and local ones, that had started sending aid at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I interrupted you where you continued your answer, starting with, "When I mentioned Mr. Krajisnik and even myself ..." Could I ask you to take up your answer from there and continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, on several occasions, asked General Milovanovic to react as quickly as possible, and to allow for a safe passage to these convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did they ever oppose or did they ever turn down such a request? Perhaps I should ask you about General Milovanovic because you're mainly talking about him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes there were lengthy discussions because, as I've already said, the generals found it difficult sometimes to react to a telephone request or a verbal request or a verbal description, describing as to what needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's procedure [Realtime transcript read in error "Let's proceed here"] but as far as the content is concerned. The transcript says "Let's proceed here," but it's: "That is procedure." That is, do I need written documents or can I act on a telephone message? But as far as the content of it was concerned, whether or not to let the convoy through.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already told you, sometimes there were problems in letting convoys or lorries through. Sometimes those were not convoys but single lorries, and I suppose that those lorries had their escorts. So in your answer, I can say -- in your question, I can answer yes, there were problems when the military simply didn't want to react in a positive way. And as I've already told you, they would ask for a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And finally, if they were against letting through a convoy or a truck, finally, did they ever refuse, at the very end, to let it through, or if they got the written instructions or whatever piece of paper they would need, would they finally, despite their opposition, do what they were requested to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once they received a piece of paper, as far as I know, the convoys were allowed to go through. They were not stopped. When I say "convoys," I also refer to a single lorry, whatever was in question, so all those could go through. But sometimes they had to wait until the paper was issued, taken over to them, enclosed with the request. So sometimes convoys or lorries would have to wait, which was not beneficial to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the reasons for opposition on the part of General Milovanovic, and I don't know whether it would be true for General Mladic as well, would these be military considerations, such as, well, the situation on the ground militarily needs not to be disturbed by any convoys or any trucks going through, or would there be other reasons such as, "Why do they need humanitarian aid? We don't see the need for that." I mean, the opposition could be for various reasons. Could you tell us, in those discussions, what kind of -- what the reasons for their opposition was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only quote General Milovanovic from memory because I most often spoke to him. And he would say, "How do I know what is in the lorry, in the convoy or in whatever?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I understand this to be that the nature of the opposition was the uncertainty about the -- what was in the trucks and what was in the convoy which could create a military risk or -- is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. More or less. That would be the correct understanding, because I suppose - and I know - that some of those lorries were sealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, in 1992, when you were in Pale, did you ever hear of a body called the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I really don't remember any such body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- after you moved to Mali Dom, and you told the Trial Chamber this afternoon that you did work in connection with the National Assembly, who did you, if there was somebody you reported to, who did you report to in your work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it came to the so-called press clippings or press summaries, they were based on the printed matter that we could get hold of, I would give those to Mr. Krajisnik, because at the time I was officially affiliated with the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you do other work in connection with the National Assembly apart from your work in relation to press materials?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the sessions of the National Assembly always implied that no matter where people were employed, they had to be nearby in order to help with the technical and administrative work. However, I cannot say with any degree of certainty whether during that short period of time there were any sessions or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you involved with what you described as the technical and administrative work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in that. When sessions were held and while I worked with Professor Koljevic, the few of us had to be there to help out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So -- well, without in the first place going into too much detail, what was the nature of the technical and administrative work with which you helped?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if a session of the National Assembly was taking place - and I'm referring to the period when I worked with Professor Koljevic - there were no mobile phones, and communication channels were not so good, so sometimes we had to act as couriers, we had to distribute materials, we had to count votes, because there were no technical means to replace human work. And also, Professor Koljevic later on liked me to be around.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you've referred in that last answer to the period when you worked with Professor Koljevic. Could you -- could you explain when and how you came to work for Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The short period of time during which I prepared reports and press summaries was the time when Mr. Koljevic did not have his own office or his own service at his disposal. Mr. Krajisnik then asked me to come and told me that I would be the best person for Professor Koljevic because Professor Koljevic did not have anybody that would help him out. He didn't have a service. Mr. Krajisnik then helped him and organised matters so that Professor Koljevic could have an office of his own, and then Professor Koljevic and I started working together on the second floor of this small building called Mali Dom. First we shared an office, and later on we moved to a bigger office. Since Mrs. Plavsic spent most of her time in Belgrade and would arrive only rarely, she would use that one small office and Professor Koljevic and I moved to the offices above Mr. Krajisnik's office, also on the second floor. That is when I got my office and Professor Koljevic had an office of his own. And we were separated only by a very narrow hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So how long after you had moved to Mali Dom do you say it was that you began then to work in that way for Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a few weeks later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in those few weeks, then, before you went to work for Professor Koljevic, did you work in the same office as Mr. Krajisnik, in a similar way to the way in which you had worked at Kikinda?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, there was a very, very small office. Mr. Krajisnik's office was to the right, as you came up the stairs, and the small office that I'm referring to was to the left. It was very, very small and we used to call it the ICU room.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, is that an acronym or -- is that in English?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was so small that we had to name it. So we called it a shock room. It was rather claustrophobic and small.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you able, during that time at Mali Dom, were you able to form an impression of how Mr. Krajisnik's working day was spent; on what sort of matters, with what people?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of people came from everywhere. There were deputies who came, the vice-president of the Assembly was also in the same building. There were a lot of international meetings, as it were, with UNPROFOR, with various liaison officers, and I was very much aware of the fact that when I moved to work with Professor Koljevic, there were Karadzic's brainstorming sessions because of which we were all forced to stay at work late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the length of a typical working day for Mr. Krajisnik at that time was what?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, like everybody else save for Mr. Karadzic, who came to work a bit later - he arrived at nine, or by nine the latest - and sometimes we would say until 2, 3, or 4.00 in the morning on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, when you worked for Professor Koljevic, were you in a position to observe and know with any closeness what work he did?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic liked to gather people around him. The commissioners would come to see Professor Koljevic, the commissioners for certain regions, before those were abolished. Mr. Nikola Poplasen, Mr. Radovanovic, Mr. Jovanovic. They would all come. Djokanovic, of course. Professor Koljevic also spoke to UNPROFOR, and he was the president of the state body for cooperation with the UN and the international humanitarian organisations, while I was the secretary of that body. However, I'm talking about a body that was established at a later stage, but even before that, Professor Koljevic had contacts with all these organisations. There were also international mediators, negotiators, foreign journalists, who wanted to interview him. It was easy to talk to him because he spoke really good English. In other words, he was active from early morning to late in the evening, and I repeat that Dr. Karadzic called those famous meetings of his in his office and that took up a lot of our evenings, and he did that because Dr. Karadzic's biorhythm was somewhat different than everybody else's; he liked to work in the evening and during the night. He was a night owl.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Nikola Poplasen. Did he have some specific area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, Nikola Poplasen was the commissioner for Vogosca, Ilijas, and those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the -- so far as you were aware, what was the nature of his contact or dealings with Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all came to deliver verbal reports as to what was going on, on the ground, what the situation was like, what the atmosphere was. That was more or less it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Deliver verbal reports to whom?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily to Professor Koljevic. Actually, when we shared that one office, I attended all those meetings. This just could not be avoided. We had to share the same place when these people came, and we talked. However, those were verbal reports and, truth be told, I can't remember a single written report that was given to Professor Koljevic. Maybe only Dragan Djokanovic used some written forms of reporting, as far as I can remember, and the others didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When Mr. Poplasen reported to Professor Koljevic in the way you described and you said you attended those meetings, was Mr. Krajisnik present?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was -- you mentioned Mr. Radovanovic as well. Do you remember his first name?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did he have a particular area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. But believe me, as I sit here, I can't remember what was his area. I'm sure of Djokanovic, Poplasen, Jovanovic and what their areas were, but I don't know what Radovanovic was in charge of because I have to tell you that this was sheer escapism, escape from reality. We chatted about this and that and the other more than anything else. These were not serious meetings that had to have an agenda, of which records had to be kept or any such thing. Those who knew Professor Koljevic obviously will understand that style of work, if I may call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'll come back to that in a moment, if I may. Can I just go on to specifics for a moment? You said you did remember Mr. Jovanovic's area of responsibility. What was that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Dragan Djokanovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area around the Drina, Bratunac, Skelani, and that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said at the very end of your previous answer, "Those who knew Professor Koljevic obviously will understand that style of work ..." Well, because you're the witness, Mrs. Cenic, and you were there, could you enlighten the Trial Chamber as to what that style of work was that would lead to an understanding.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic liked to talk about culture, of course, about Shakespeare, about literature, about people in general. So that very often he would escape and try to find a resort on those topics. People that I have mentioned knew him even before the war, before all of these events, so the tone of their conversation was always of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we take it that -- I'm being serious in this introduction, that however much discussion there was about Shakespeare or literature in these meetings, that these men, Poplasen, Djokanovic, Jovanovic, Radovanovic, they were at least attempting to report and convey to Professor Koljevic something about what was going on in their areas of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With the proviso that these oral reports lasted for perhaps half an hour, and the remainder of the time - and these meetings were sometimes longish - was dedicated to topics from the field of culture or about what to do next. Professor Koljevic had ideas about organising different cultural and educational events. The remainder of the conversation had to do with these topics and such topics. Only half an hour would be used for reports about the state of affairs, the situation, the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So there would, would there, be some report about the situation on the ground in the particular municipalities concerned?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you recall whether that included reports or information about the military situation?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as it was called at the time, the security situation in these municipalities, and the related problems were discussed. That's to say the actual events in these municipalities, numbers of those killed. That would be it for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there discussion or report at those -- at these meetings about population movements?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was discussion about that too, and about the quality of people's lives, how many people there were in the municipalities, the problem caused by the fact that the people kept leaving municipalities, that there was this outflow of population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that outflow, did that relate to outflow of just one ethnic group or more than one ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular period of time, the Muslim or, rather, Bosniak population, as well as the Croat population, was scarce. As far as I remember, the problem consisted in the fact that the Serbs started leaving as well. Another difficulty was posed by the fact that refugees or displaced persons kept arriving from other municipalities with all the problems that they experienced. The situation was rather odd and quite serious. The local population was leaving and there was the influx of the populations from other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, are you -- in that last description, I'd just like to be clear. Are you talking about Pale or are you talking about the municipalities that were the areas of responsibility of these gentlemen who visited Dr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking in general terms about the areas from which these commissioners originated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you remember -- I take it that at some point in your life you have heard the phrase "ethnic cleansing." Just a yes -- just asking you whether you have ever heard that phrase.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This coined phrase of such grievous substance was imparted to me or, rather, I heard it from foreign journalists because, until then, we had been discussing refugees when we were referring in general terms to all of us in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you remember when you first heard that phrase?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of autumn, when contacts with the people from the outside, the contacts that I had, became more frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So by the time of these meetings with Mr. Poplasen, Radovanovic, Jovanovic and Djokanovic and Professor Koljevic, by the time those meetings began, had you by then heard this phrase?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, before Professor Koljevic and I started working together, I had heard of this accusation of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What did you -- at the time, what did you understand it to mean?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it to mean an accusation that members of the Bosniak population were being forced or were under pressure to leave their homes, as were members of the Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you any reason to doubt that, by the time these meetings began, Professor Koljevic was as familiar with that phrase as you were?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I expressed my question clumsily. By the time these meetings began, do you consider that Professor Koljevic was as familiar with that phrase as you were?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Koljevic frequently interacted with international organisations and authorities, including foreign journalists. Naturally, he was often asked that same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did any question of ethnic cleansing come up in any of the meetings with those four men; Poplasen, Radovanovic, Jovanovic, Djokanovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentlemen I mentioned, including Mr. Koljevic and myself, all of us were refugees as well. That's to say we had all moved away from our homes. And we all found it hard to understand this accusation, which had to do with ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my -- is this to be an affirmative answer? The question was whether any question of ethnic cleansing came up in any of the meetings. Should I conclude from your answer that it did, where you said that you all found it hard to understand this accusation, that you discussed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentlemen I'm referring to also read about ethnic cleansing and about accusations that there was ethnic cleansing underway, and discussed it. We discussed it amongst ourselves. As I said, we found it hard to fathom the accusation in view of the fact that we had all moved out of our homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask you a question? I can imagine, if you say "I moved out of my house," would that exclude, in your opinion, or in the opinion of those who you're talking about at that moment, that a similar thing happened to Bosniaks or Muslims elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We were of the opinion -- I was of the opinion too -- that the same misfortune befell others who were forced to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Including Muslims, Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Including Bosniaks, Croats, Jews, Gypsies; all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let me just reread your answer. You said you had all moved out of -- "... we had all moved out of our homes." Was that moving out because you were forced to do so, either by persons or circumstances, or was it your own free will to say, well, I'd rather move out of my house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was by no means of my own free will, or anyone other's, for that matter. I am still homesick about my Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said that the same misfortune befell others who were forced to leave their homes. You said so in answer to my question whether you would exclude that the same happened to others. Were you aware at that time that this happened to these others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because the makeup of municipalities changed completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- yes, but -- and you thought it was due to similar moving out, that is not voluntarily moving out, people perhaps being as homesick as you were, in these other municipalities? Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe everyone wanted to return to their homes, just as I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you moved out due to pressure or circumstances or -- what happened to you? I mean, I'm seeking the comparison to what you thought happened to others as well. Could you be a bit more precise? Was life miserable? Were you forced out at gunpoint? What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the apartment block where I lived, where my parents had an apartment, already by that time there were no people left there. The apartment block had been shot at, there were armies and uniforms that I had never seen before, and members of this army wearing the sort of uniform were seen entering the apartment block and were seen around it. It wasn't even safe to open the front door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this -- was your apartment situated such that it could have been for military purposes that these members of the army were entering the apartment block?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, in early April, I don't really know what was important strategically and militarily in and around that building. So I don't see really why a uniformed person, and particularly a person wearing black or green camouflage uniform, would be entering the building armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can I understand this as that you considered that to be intimidation by armed forces against those who were living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were civilians living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period of time, some of the families had already left the building. Of course, there were still quite a few civilians who continued living there, especially so because the ethnic makeup of the residents in the apartment block where I had grown up was also mixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to return to one of your earlier questions, when you were asked about the outflow. Mr. Stewart asked you about whether population movements were discussed, and you said -- the question then was, was that outflow, did that relate to outflow of just one ethnic group or more than one ethnic group? And then you answered: "In this particular period of time, the Muslim or, rather, Bosniak population, as well as the Croat population, was scarce. As far as I remember, the problem consisted in the fact that the Serbs started leaving as well." I have some difficulties in fully understanding your answer. When you said -- and let's go it portion by portion. You said the Bosniak as well as the Croatian population was scarce.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were in a minority, both the Bosniak and Croat population. Some of the Serbs had also gone to Serbia and what then happened was that Serbs continued leaving in an organised fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the next question was whether that description, whether it was just about Pale or whether this was -- whether you were talking about the municipalities that were the areas of responsibilities of these gentlemen, and then you said, "I'm talking general terms about the areas from which these commissioners originated." Is this is to say that there was no outflow of Bosniaks and Croats from any of these areas which -- well, it's a considerable outflow or considerable movement of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, by that time, considerable numbers, although I can't give you an exact percentage, but definitely more than half of Croats and Bosniaks, had left the area. When I'm talking about the population moving out, I wanted to say that the local population continued gradually to move out, so their numbers steadily decreased. However, at the same time refugees from other municipalities were arriving in the area. This resulted in problems because they arrived there practically with nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You two times said "the area." Which area exactly did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These areas, I'm talking about Herzegovina, Vogosca and Ilijas were areas that I mentioned earlier on, and the area of Bratunac, Skelani, that general area too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you made a comparison between your fate and the fate of Muslims and Croats. You just told us that -- let me just find your words literally. When you said more than half of Croats and Bosniaks had left the area --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Areas. Would that be over the whole of the territory, both Bosniak-controlled and Serb-controlled or would that just be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can talk in general terms in this context. This applies to Bosnia-Herzegovina, all across the board, because hardly anyone stayed behind in the same area where they resided. At least this was rarely the case as of April 1992 onwards. I had met people from different parts of the country who were on the move, who had moved away from their homes, for these misfortunate circumstances, to call them that way. Also -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. You said "also".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just as Banja Luka was no longer Banja Luka, Sarajevo was no longer Sarajevo. Not a single town in Bosnia-Herzegovina was what it used to be. Perhaps with the exception of some which were predominantly mono-ethnic in terms of their population, but then these towns again experienced an influx of population and consequently must have gone through a change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that if parts of the population would move out from other areas people would move in. Just to see whether I well understood your testimony, you described how by intimidation, you were forced to leave where you lived. And you compared your situation with the situation of Muslims and Croats who left from the places where they lived and you told, I think, of similar circumstances. That means also by -- intimidated by the situation that they would leave their area just as you had left yours. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding was, at the time, that people who were leaving felt insecure wherever they were, regardless of their ethnicity, and were merely seeking security and safety for them and -- themselves and their families. It's difficult for me to say who was worse off, who was better off, when we are talking about individual fates. But this was and is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you find it difficult to make a comparison who was better off, who was worse off, but if we are talking about these movements of population, was that, since you talked about changing of the composition in certain municipalities, changing of the composition of -- ethnic composition of the population, that this was large-scale movement or medium-scale or small-scale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on the town, probably. I think that most of the people were in search of security and safety. That was the case in 1992 and definitely also in 1993. Therefore, the moving out of the population did not take place on such a large scale in 1992 because based on the information I had about the whereabouts of the people at the time, the people hoped that matters would be settled quite soon. Later on, as I started working in this state committee and after the accords were signed in particular, and after the statement of the chief of the Red Cross for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Somarruga, there were requests to the effect that the non-Serb population be allowed to move out of the Krajina. I know because in 1993, I was faced with this problem, practically on a daily basis. It was at that time that I became aware of the numbers of people who were leaving or trying to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to take Sarajevo and Pale for example where you moved out, in 1992, by the end of 1992, were the majority of Serbs that used to live in what was now a Bosnian Muslim-controlled Sarajevo still there, or had most of them left that part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Sarajevo was a specific case and a very difficult case, because those more fortunate ones left on time, as it were. However, many Serbs stayed in Sarajevo, hoping that eventually they would be able to leave. I know because I myself participated in a number of activities aimed at establishing contact with these people in order to help them, either through UNPROFOR or through some private channels. A lot of families were split. They would come to our offices in Pale with dozens of requests a day, asking us to help them to get hold of their families in Sarajevo and to help them transfer either to Pale or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you consider it to be wrong that you were not protected in the place where you lived, and that you were in such a way intimidated that you had to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. None of us would probably ever recover from that feeling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we have now talked about population movements and Sarajevo being different, Serbs moving out, Muslims and Croats moving out from where they lived, depending on the municipality, whether these were larger or smaller numbers. Did you discuss these matters among yourselves? That's with the persons you earlier mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With sadness and with nostalgia, all of us spoke with a lot of emotions, especially during those years because we had all been through the same life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you spoken with -- well, let's say a representative or at least members of the other nationalities or ethnicities after the war about these -- about what you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is also the nature of my job, and whatever I have been involved in over the past few years is dedicated to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I often talk to my colleagues as well as to my friends, in an attempt to prevent something like this ever happening to any of us again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you -- did you experience that Muslims and Croats you've talked to had similar feelings as you have, that is being sad that they had to leave and could you understand that, if they did express such feelings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I understand them and, of course, I have listened to their sad stories. They had been through the same things as all of us and we have arrived at a conclusion that there is a lot of grounds for comparison in how each of us felt during the various stages of war. First of all, there came disbelief. Then rage. Then anger. Then sadness. There was also hope. And those feelings took turns. And I think that the stories are the same, stories told by Serbs as well as the Bosniaks, as well as the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Looking at the clock, Mr. Stewart, I took quite some time. I'm aware. If you would say "you interrupted me," but I would nevertheless like to put a few additional questions. We have limited time. If you would say we could restart after the break, then we'll restart after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's no problem at all for me, Your Honour. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until 20 minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, you've mentioned those -- I won't repeat the names all over again, those four particular men who came to visit Mr. Koljevic as you described. Were there others in addition to those four in a similar position in relation to other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina that came to see him?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any others in a similar or same position. I remember the people that I have mentioned very well, and I remember their visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I forgot to mention something. You did it any way, actually, Mrs. Cenic. I've been asked to ask if you could just pause after my question because you're hearing my question in English. Maybe somebody told you because you did it naturally then any way. So -- but if you could do that it would be helpful, thank you. The -- when -- so let's stick with those four, then. When any of those four gentlemen was there with Professor Koljevic, was -- did Professor Koljevic express any concerns with any of them about ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, for all of us, including Professor Koljevic, those were accusations that made no sense to us whatsoever. Professor Koljevic, himself a displaced person, a refugee, shared that opinion. Professor Koljevic and myself spent a lot of time together. The only time we didn't spend together was when he attended meetings without me and in the evenings when we said our good nights to go to bed, and while we were together, we spoke about this quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- what did you understand, at its highest, its worst, what did you understand the accusation against Serbs to be?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We understood at the time that the accusation implied that all this was part of some plan, this ethnic cleansing, and that is why we were absolutely baffled by this accusation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if it were, just for the moment, if it were or had been some plan, what did you understand the accusation to involve, as far as the actions in implementation of that plan were concerned?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't fully understand your question, with regard to the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it, then, Mrs. Cenic. If there was, which you're saying was the accusation, there was some plan to commit ethnic cleansing, that's -- that's what you're saying, you're not saying it happened but you're saying that's the starting point of the accusation, agreed? Just trying to set the base line.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such plan, nor did I ever see it. I never came across such a plan. That's one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And secondly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Pause for a moment, Mrs. Cenic. I'm having difficulty making myself clear here. If there is a plan -- please just bear with me for a moment. If there is a plan, it's a plan to do something, rights? So what I'm getting at, if it was a plan to commit ethnic cleansing, the concept of ethnic cleansing, what did you understand the accusation to be? That there was a plan by the Bosnian Serbs, obviously? There was a plan to do something which constituted ethnic cleansing. What did you understand the accusation to be, as to what was to be done? What was it said that there was a plan to do?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that there was a plan to systematically expel, by force, or by other means, all those who were of non-Serb origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever, in 1992, read or hear of anything to support the accusation that there was such a plan by Bosnian Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In particular, did Professor Koljevic ever say anything to you to imply any recognition or concern or fear on his part that there might be such a plan by any of the Bosnian Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Professor Koljevic ever say to you or suggest to you that Mr. Krajisnik had any different idea, different plan, different policy, from Professor Koljevic's own, in relation to any such matters of population movements approached at other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Professor Koljevic ever suggest to you that in any way Mr. Krajisnik was aggressive, war mongering, in any way?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did he ever make any comment or any suggestion to you that Mr. Krajisnik was not committed to peaceful resolution of conflict, as far as it could be achieved?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If any such thing had been the case, I would not be sitting here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So just to clarify, if any suggestion of any of those matters had ever come to you from Professor Koljevic, did you know of anything to support such a suggestion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, ever did Professor Koljevic suggest in any way that his way of thinking differs from Mr. Krajisnik's way of thinking, especially when it came to the numerous efforts to negotiate in order to find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any discussion at any of these meetings with any of those four gentlemen, Mr. Poplasen and the other three, with Professor Koljevic, was there any discussion which suggested any cover-up to protect anybody present at that meeting or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you implying that something was hidden, was covered up?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I'm asking whether -- I'm not implying, I'm asking whether there was any discussion about or with a view to any such cover-up.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what was said in my presence. And I never gained an impression that there was a cover-up, that something was being hidden. Moreover, please bear in mind that those people were commissioners, that they would go to their respective territories and they would come back. For example, Mr. Poplasen was not in Vogosca and Ilijas all the time. He would just go there and then he would return, after having spent some time there, a few days, at the most. He would then come back and return to his area. This is -- this was the procedure. This is what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- at those meetings, did any of those four men raise any questions or make any reports as to the degree of discipline and control in the areas for which they were responsible?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were comments to that effect. And it was said that a lot of people, a lot of groups, I don't know what else to call them, were not under the control of the military, under any command, for that matter, and that they exerted a very bad influence on the overall situation, which was rather difficult as it was. That was one of the issues that were discussed at the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How would you compare, if you can, the working relationship at that time between, on the one hand, Mr. Poplasen and Professor Koljevic, and on the other hand, Mr. Poplasen and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the relation between Poplasen and Krajisnik, I don't know anything about it because I never saw them together at a meeting. I didn't, and I can't vouch for anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If I ask you the same question but in relation to Mr. Djokanovic, is your answer the same or different?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic was much closer to Professor Koljevic, and that relationship existed when I came to Pale, because I used to see them together. And as a result of that, we quite often joked at Mr. Djokanovic's expense and I'm not aware of any meetings that took place between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Djokanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I get a bit confused. Your first question was about relation between Mr. Poplasen and Professor Koljevic on the one hand and Mr. Poplasen and Mr. Krajisnik on the other hand. That question was answered half, only in relation to Mr. Poplasen and Krajisnik. Then you asked the same question but in relation to Mr. Djokanovic. Then I take it Mr. Poplasen and Mr. Djokanovic or did you mean to say Djokanovic and Krajisnik and Koljevic? And then the answer was that Djokanovic was much closer to Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I could -- I could lead probably to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I had thought, I confess I had thought -- well, this is not an unintelligent witness, Your Honour. I had thought she would -- I didn't need to elaborate the question. She seemed, with respect, to understand it clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the first question, at least, she answered only half.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, I was asking her to draw a comparison. Since she didn't know anything about one half of the comparison, she did in effect answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Although the -- let me just reread the answer to the second question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm happy to seek to clarify it or invite Your Honour to. I really don't mind at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I clarify, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, yes, you may. Perhaps that's the quickest way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was going to say, Your Honour, the witness could save us both the trouble.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the Poplasen-Krajisnik relationship is concerned, I don't know what the nature of that relationship was because I never attended or saw the two of them in a meeting, and I can't say whether their relationship was good or bad or anything else because I don't know anything about that relationship and I never attended a meeting, I never saw a meeting between Krajisnik and Poplasen. I personally didn't, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The matter is sufficiently clear to me. For neither of them a proper comparison could be made. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I just for one moment, then, explore that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any meetings that took place between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Djokanovic so it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well Your Honour with respect the answer at page 34, line 22, you answered, Mrs. Cenic, you said Mr. Djokanovic was much closer to Professor Koljevic, closer to Professor Koljevic than what?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your earlier question was about the Poplasen-Koljevic relationship than about the Djokanovic-Koljevic relationship. The comparison was between Poplasen and Djokanovic. Djokanovic was much closer to Koljevic than Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In these meetings with the four men, I appreciate from your answers you're not saying they were all four there all there at once, perhaps we ought to clarify that. The -- we mentioned the four men, Poplasen, Djokanovic and so on. The meetings always took place, did they, with just one of them there at one time?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes they were all together but it was more like socialising. Radovanovic and Poplasen, that is, together. These were informal encounters more than anything else. Because we had no other life than that linked with these offices. Thus, the two of them would sometimes go and have a cup of coffee and chat together. Mr. Djokanovic would normally arrive on his own. On several occasions, I believe Jovanovic and Radovanovic also spent time together, but again in an informal conversation in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, at that -- these meetings in which I'll embrace all the meetings between Professor Koljevic and one or more of these men at which you were present, was there any discussion of ill-treatment of Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Prisoners were never the subject of discussion, nor were prisons in general for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were any prisons specifically the subject of discussion at any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, in your questions, are detention facilities perhaps, not being proper prisons, are they contained in your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps I will do it this way. I'm using "prisons," intending to use "prisons" in the broadest sense to include any sort of prison camp, any detention facility, basically anywhere people are kept against their will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So on that basis, prisons in that broadest sense, were any either generally or specifically were prisons the subject of discussion at any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- during what period, in so far as you can remember, from -- well, to date, during what period did such meetings between Professor Koljevic and one or more of those four men take place?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These meetings were no longer held in late autumn. Toward the end of the year. Mr. Djokanovic would still visit relatively frequently, but the meetings as such, as far as I remember, were no longer held toward the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When did they begin?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I would see, and I'm saying this because at the time I wasn't working with Professor Koljevic, I would see Professor himself. On my arrival at Pale, I would see him with Mr. Poplasen, because Mr. Poplasen spent nights at the Kikinda facility where he was put up in a room. At the time, I also saw the Professor frequently with Dragan Djokanovic. When I started working with Professor Koljevic, in the office, as I described before, I would see the four of them arriving independently of each other, as I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to come back to asking you something about Mr. Krajisnik. In your evidence on Tuesday, I think it was, you described how, on occasions, people would arrive and they would be kept waiting to see Mr. Krajisnik because he was tied up with something else. Was Mr. Krajisnik, for somebody turning up unannounced -- was Mr. Krajisnik a hard man to get to see?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How would you put it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply the way I put it before. As different people came to visit, some of them had to wait for him to be able to receive them. Therefore, he didn't refuse to meet up with anyone. It was simply the matter of time or, rather, when he would be able to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Krajisnik say something like "oh, I don't want to talk to him or I don't want to talk to her, or I'm not going to meet them"?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never said anything of the sort to me personally, to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Krajisnik express any derogatory sentiments or thoughts about other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you that had I heard from him a single discriminatory sentence against anyone, even the Martians, I would not be sitting today as I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- when you were working in Pale in the period you described in 1992, can you recall Mr. Krajisnik receiving visits from any significant members of other ethnic groups, non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Pale is concerned, there were telephone calls from people of other ethnicities, who were in search of their family members, and they called Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During that period, do you remember Mr. Krajisnik receiving visits from significant people from the Serb community but not SDS members?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people, not all of them carried their membership cards along. I never asked them about their membership, and I really don't know who was or was not a member. People came, talked, and then left. Whether one or the other was a member or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From everything that you saw and heard during that late summer and autumn in Pale, did you form any impression as to the degree of control and authority that the SDS leaders in Pale had over municipalities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't wish to speculate about what the SDS members controlled and to what extent, if so. I can only tell you that as far as Serbs are concerned, they were the strongest party with the largest membership. I also know that in quite a few municipalities, they held high positions. Moreover, many of them became SDS members only later, in 1993 in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not entirely sure that my question was a hundred per cent clear to you, Mrs. Cenic, for which I apologise. I was asking you not about the degree of control that SDS members had within the municipalities but, if you'd formed an impression as to the degree of control or authority among the SDS leadership in Pale over what was happening in other municipalities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back then and now, I state that they did not have great control because the problem was, back then, and is today, in this so-called second-rate people who mounted this sort of blockade, vis-a-vis the ordinary folk, the mortals, so to speak. I thought then, and I think now, that they were not aware of the -- of most of the things that were happening at the time on the ground, as we used to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In that answer, who did you have in mind when you referred to this so-called second-rate people?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are people who get affiliated with any sort of authority in power, with the sole purpose of doing good for themselves and bad for others. To put it simply, there are numerous examples, such people, when they came to Pale, they most often said the things they thought the authorities wanted to hear and not the things as they indeed were. Furthermore, this is something I know, during these visits there was always the same team of people receiving the leadership, and I believe that almost never, to the best of my knowledge, in 90 per cent of the cases, what they were saying was not the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, when you said in that answer during these visits, you're talking about visits by people from other municipalities to Pale or Pale leaders to municipalities, or both?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to both these cases. As far as the visits are concerned, they most often took place during Assembly sessions or, for instance, Professor Koljevic and I would visit Banja Luka, when we would always be met by this welcoming committee of the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And just to clarify, when you talked about so-called second-rate people who mounted this sort of blockade, you're talking about blockade in the figurative sense to describe what you've just dealt with in the last couple of answers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. I repeat: Quite a few of them were people interested in their careers only, and who in most of the cases only said things that were expected to be heard from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I seek some clarifications? If you're talking about these second-rate people, would they be SDS members or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of them were not SDS members at the time. They would become members eventually. Some of them had been SDS members from before the war. For others, I don't know their membership, and most probably they themselves didn't know whose members they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you gave the example of the committee that would receive -- I understand the leadership in Banja Luka. Could you tell us, just give us the names of the members on this committee and could you tell us whether they were SDS members, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In giving you an example, perhaps I should use the example of Banja Luka and Krajina. In the case of Banja Luka, there were always Mr. Radic, Mr. Kasagic, Dr. Vukic, Mrs. Hrvacanin on several occasions. Therefore, there were always these same people. And I don't think Professor Koljevic ever had the occasion to talk to other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, which of those you mentioned were not SDS members, which of them were SDS members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of the ones that I mentioned now, well, I believe they were members even before the war. Some of them became members later, like some of the ministers in the government, who became members as they assumed their duties, because, as they put it, it was quite logical to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed. Yes, Judge Hanoteau was a question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry, Madam, to ask you to put your headphones on but I wanted to ask you a question, it's a sort of a general question. Answering to a question of Mr. Stewart, put to you by Mr. Stewart, you described to us the person that Mr. Krajisnik is, described how he was when the visitors came to see him. You talked to us about what he would say with regard to other members of other ethnic communities. I wanted to ask you the following question: Did you ever hear Mr. Krajisnik deny that things were happening? Did you ever hear him protest against things that were happening or condemn things that were happening around him, or to say something against the choices that people had taken? Did you ever hear him express any regret with regard to what was going on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On several occasions, Mr. Krajisnik was angry because of the various groups that toured the areas and did evil things indeed. Whoever was in a position to inform about this, for instance I myself, I don't know about others, if we had coffee or as Mr. Krajisnik called it, our heroic strong coffee, I myself had occasion to inform him about things that I learnt were happening. Mr. Krajisnik was always angry about things that were being done to people in the name of something. Furthermore, Mr. Krajisnik always insisted that people be treated with respect, and I believe he illustrated that in the case of my own family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What would you tell him? Can you tell us what is it that you would hear and you would tell him, for instance? You said, "I myself had occasion to tell them about things that I learnt were happening."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for example, the instances around Ilijas, where evidently there was a paramilitary formation in existence, which, or rather the members of which were of frightful appearance because they had frightening signs on them like skulls and things like that which frightened the population. I was in a position to talk to Mr. Krajisnik about this, and his reaction was anger, because these people were under nobody's command. As Mr. Krajisnik would put it, nobody has the right to do anything evil in the name of the Serbian people, nor to frighten people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there any room for manoeuvre? Did he do something, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went out of the office and I suppose he did, since he was giving instructions to his secretary, telling her to get him on the phone with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question for you, Madam.
