Given what you told us regarding this first part of your activities when you were in charge of paper clippings and newspaper clippings and, of course, I'm going back to the beginning of your testimony of today, did you have a television set in your offices anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There wasn't a television set either in Mr. Krajisnik's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, no, I don't think so. I really can't remember. I'm trying to remember when it was that we received PCs. I remember that I was still typing on a typewriter, and no, I don't think there was one, no. Not in the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Kikinda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after? At Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't there at Jahorina. We went over to Mali Dom, and as I said, I was in this small office at Mali Dom. Later on, we had television sets, but that was later. I don't even think that we had them in that same year, because, as I said, we first received PCs after we had had only typewriters, and perhaps only later, a TV set was installed somewhere. Later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You cannot tell us when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Really, I don't know whether this was towards the end of that year or in 1993. I really don't remember when the TV was installed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question has to deal with one of your answers. You've told us that you've never heard talk about detention centres, prisons, or of any such place while you were working for Mr. Koljevic. Did you yourself know that these detention centres existed? When did you find out about their existence personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to make a correction. I said that no prisons, detention units, or any thing of that sort was a subject of discussion with the four gentlemen who came to the office and who had questions addressed to them. I never said that I never heard or knew that they existed. I only said that with those four gentlemen, there was no discussion about them. As for the detention units, camps, collection centres, I heard of them, and in my testimony, I've already mentioned that at the beginning of that autumn, in September, I went to one of those places with the journalist whom I mentioned. Also, during the summer of that year, stories about Prijedor reached us. And then a visit was organised because international representatives asked for that visit. I particularly remember the visit of a gentleman from abroad who was either a sir or a lord. I'm not sure. And I remember when he went there with the deputy health minister in order to inspect the area of Prijedor. As for prisons and detention units, yes, they were mentioned that summer because lists for exchanges arrived with the names of people on those lists, and the person who was involved in that was Mr. Momcilo Mandic. Sometimes I would be the one to receive those faxes, and as far as the Croatian side is concerned, I believe that the counterpart's family name was Plejic, Mr. Plejic. On behalf of the Croats or Herceg-Bosnia the Croats there played an official role. However, he resided in Frankfurt, and that's where he called from when it came to the exchanges of the people on those lists. So already at that time, I did hear about detention units, and I have just now described how I heard of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask one follow-up question there. You said that there was no television set in Mr. Krajisnik's office. We heard evidence about the presence of satellite television with reception of, for example, CNN, in Pale, from someone who worked there during 1992, periods of 1992. Are you aware of the presence of any satellite television facility, whether it was in the office or next to the office, of -- whether it would be Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, or do you say, no, there was no television reception which was able to receive international channels at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never heard of satellite television before. There is the first time I hear any such thing. As for television sets, people had them at their homes. It is possible that there was a television set in that facility because this was a holiday place. However, I did not see any television sets in any of the offices. I did not have a television set in my office, for the short period of time that I was involved in preparing press clippings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "that facility"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Kikinda building. It is possible that there was a television set there, just an ordinary TV set. But not in the office. This had been a holiday place before, and I'm sure that they had had television sets or a television set, in the holiday place. However, during the day, we did not watch TV at work. People had television sets in their own private houses and they watched those channels that could be received. When we moved to the Mali Dom building, in the office that I occupied, there was no TV set. Later on -- but I don't know whether it was in 1992 or in 1993, honestly, I can't remember, we received TV sets. We received them in the Mali Dom building as well. Now, as for the satellite dish or any satellite channels, believe me, at the time, I could not follow any of them. I did not have an opportunity to see, to watch any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- I do understand that you do say I could not follow any of them, I did not have an opportunity. But would you exclude for the possibility that satellite television was received in, well, let's say, government or related premises? That means government, Assembly, officers working for the government or for the Assemblies -- for the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that I never saw a satellite TV in the Kikinda building, ever. Never ever did I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you earlier told us that through press clippings you would gather information of what was published. Sometimes it was even taken by couriers to Pale so there seemed to have been an interest knowing what was published about the situation. How do you explain that where satellite television is -- let me say it, one of the relatively simple technical means of finding out what is broadcast about the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, why -- how could you explain that no one ever thought, well, this is a way to get information just as we tried to gather that from press clippings? It's far easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it took me a while, and luckily enough, Mr. Krajisnik appreciated that, to explain that we needed at least PCs for our work, and to explain why a scanner would be important for our work. Even for that, one had to have means and ways to obtain that equipment. I fully appreciate that things would have been much easier with a satellite TV, but I did not have it. I did not have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I did not have access to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you did not have but since we heard evidence that CNN was watched in Pale, of course, I'm trying to understand the one testimony and the other testimony, and also to see whether there is a logical explanation for the difference in that testimony and what you tell us at this moment. But you say, in Pale, government facilities or related facilities, there was no satellite television received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Kikinda building, I did not see a satellite TV anywhere. Later on, when things went on, Mr. Karadzic had TV in his office and he could watch CNN, BBC, ABC, and others, but in the Kikinda building I never saw a satellite dish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any of the other buildings during 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, until the moment we moved to Mali Dom, I really didn't see any anywhere. And once we moved to the Mali building, Mali Dom building, in my office and the adjacent offices I did not see a satellite dish oar a satellite TV. Later on, yes. As I've already told you, later on I know that Dr. Karadzic had it in his office and that he could follow various channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was after 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there -- among the Serb community in 1992, what was their general assessment, so far as you could tell, of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to people in general and what they were saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a number of people, with all due respect to Mrs. Plavsic, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, and Mr. Krajisnik, depending on the part of the state or the part of the territory where they resided, although they enjoyed respect, a majority of common people were angry that they could not reach any of them, to tell them what was really going on, or to tell them something about those people that represented them, and their respective municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the relationship so far as you could see in 1992 between Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could hear their conversations, there was a lot of tension in their relationship, judging by the raised voices, especially the raised voice of Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you acquire any knowledge yourself of what had led to tension and raised voices?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in addition to the way they treated the procedure respective to the humanitarian aid convoys, journalists, when I say journalists, very often the arrival of journalists had to be provided with security. I know that those were some of the problems, but I was not aware of any details. I know there was also a problem regarding the so-called municipal armies, like the one that had been formed in Vogosca at the very beginning. I suppose that General Mladic's opinion on all those differed from the opinion of Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you don't know?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only superficially from what I heard in 1992. Later on, I attended a greater number of those meetings and discussions, but at that time, the time in question, those issues were only touched upon and that's why I don't know any details. In any case, that was one of the issues of their discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether General Mladic and Dr. Karadzic in 1992 saw eye-to-eye on the organisation of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never attended any of those discussions and I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the dealings between Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic, would you be able to say whether either of them was the dominant personality?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in 1992 and later on, they had very pronounced egos. It is a very big question whether any of them would have prevailed in that relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To return to a topic we left yesterday but, Your Honours, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Stewart. I don't know how much time you would still need. If you say "I need just for the topic," I don't know how many topics there are still to come but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. As best I can do, Your Honour. I think I'm looking at something like between 20 and 30 minutes or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's certainly too much for before the break. The witness was scheduled for six hours in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Estimated, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Estimated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know how long I've had because Your Honour has the computer information that I don't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking Mr. Registrar to give me the update of where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is still -- you're at 4 hours, 46 minutes, I do understand. We will adjourn until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, I was asking you yesterday, but we dropped the topic for the time being, about your visit with the Canadian journalist to Trnopolje. On your visit there, did you see anything which indicated to you that there was or had been improper treatment of anybody detained there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it strange to see so many people on this one spot, with many of their belongings scattered about. What I also found odd were these bicycles that one could see along the approach road. In general, the atmosphere was far from pleasant. Do you want me to describe it in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let me ask questions, then, Mrs. Cenic of the first of all, was it clear to you that people were being detained there against their will, at the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, because we asked the man wearing this incomplete uniform what this was all about. He told us that it was a collection centre, something of the sort. People were getting in and going out. These were women, men, wearing civilian clothes. I also found it odd to see them arrive on bicycles. I wasn't under the impression that they were prisoners, but I didn't find it normal to see them staying there either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the same question as the last time you raised the issue. Are you challenging the adjudicated facts which, of course, you're entitled to do but which would take more than it hear the testimony of someone who spent a -- perhaps couple of hours on one day. How do we have to understand this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact Your Honour puts your finger on it. If I were at any point to challenge the adjudicated facts I would -- I would need to do it on something other than the evidence which I'm proposing to adduce on this witness. I hope that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Your Honour's point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did it -- did it appear to you who was running this camp, well, who was in charge of the camp?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is because as I said, the uniform didn't have any insignia, and it wasn't clear to me who had control over it all. Evidently there was some sort of control there but I don't know who was officially in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- did you see or hear anything on that visit which you then felt it was necessary to report back to anybody when you returned to Pale?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my return to Pale, I mentioned this, but not in any sort of report, because, as I said, I wasn't required to submit any sort of reports. Still, in this -- or, rather, I talked to my colleagues about this particular leg of my journey, as I did in fact about all the other legs of this journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And which of your colleagues did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to Ms. Milijana, Ms. Milena, and the people who were working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was anything of what you then discussed with your colleagues a matter which caused you concern to the point where you felt that somebody in higher authority should know?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't submit any sort of report. I only had these conversations, because I had experienced various things during this journey. Perhaps it was only at this point that I realised that the situation was more serious than I had expected it to be or that I had thought it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- can you say what specifically was more serious than you had expected?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that I observed on this journey was more serious than I could have expected. I can illustrate this by way of several things, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, please do.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, this place called Obodni Kanal, where there was fighting at the time, there were dead bodies everywhere to be seen, and what I was particularly shocked by were these NATO packages that I was able to see in the possession of members of the Croat army. They had very well-fortified bunkers, and they left behind packages of food which was something that we didn't have. That was the first time that I saw the uniform of the army of the Republic of Croatia. Next, Bosanski Brod. Together with the Serbian army we had entered Bosanski Brod and saw columns of people. Trnopolje, where we asked to be explained who the persons there were, and what that was all about. We were told that this was a collection centre and that the people were mostly Bosniaks who were supposed to be transferred somewhere, wherever they wanted to go, abroad, and that when we saw them leave, it was because they were returning to their homes to collect some other belongings that they had left behind. To put it mildly, I found it very hard to take that -- all of that in. Then, as we went to Vogosca and Ilijas, in Ilijas, Mr. Kent, perhaps even naively, wanted to see what this demarcation line was like, that's to say the point of contact between the Bosniak and Serbian armies. We were taken, escorted to Cekrcici. However, the vehicle that was driven by a man called Damir, I don't think he's alive any more, that was driving ahead of us, was shot from a sniper. The driver was wounded, but thanks to the fact that he managed to collect his wits, we managed to run away. So there are many things which made it clear, at least to me, that the people were far from understanding the seriousness of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you -- before you went on the trip, were you discouraged in any way by anybody in Pale from going to wherever you wanted to go, wherever Mr. Kent wanted to go, or to follow up anything that Mr. Kent might be interested in?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any restrictions whatsoever or any instructions of any sort, because Mr. Kent simply wanted to see as much as he could, as he himself put it, and we travelled accordingly, according to his wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you returned to Pale, were you at any point discouraged by anyone from discussing or passing on to anybody anything which you had seen or heard on your trip with Mr. Kent?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Whatever we visited was filmed by Mr. Kent, including Derventa, which looked like a ghost town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, do you recall that during the period that you were in Pale and particularly the period that you describe where you were working at Kikinda and then at Mali Dom, that there was, as part of the Republika Srpska structure, a government, a cabinet?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was the government, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we know, nobody is going to get excited, if I put it to you that the Prime Minister was Mr. Branko Djeric. Can you say, from your knowledge, whether there were any members of that government, of that cabinet, who were effectively the more powerful, influential figures?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, those who had more power and were more prominent were Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We find, and I won't trouble everybody, including you, Mrs. Cenic, to go to the particular document, but we do find quite frequently, in minutes of government sessions at that time, a reference to somebody expressing the view that the government was receiving insufficient information. Are you able to comment usefully yourself, from what you knew at the time, as to whether that was a legitimate complaint?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour. The question is too vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first ask whether the witness has any information about what type of -- whether the government received information, what she knows about it. Could you tell us whether you have any knowledge, any personal knowledge, of -- or even indirect knowledge, of how the government was receiving information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know in what ways the government was receiving information, because I did not take part in the work of the government. Indirectly, I know that most information about matters in general were in possession of Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you any knowledge on whether they shared that information with other members of the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that with any certainty. I didn't take part in the work of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you -- have you any knowledge of -- about the flow of information between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic, on the one hand, and Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Professor Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Mr. Krajisnik is concerned, I don't know, because I didn't see them in that period of time, and I'm talking about the period I spent occupying and sharing one office with his secretary. I didn't see those gentlemen with Mr. Krajisnik. I would see Mr. Mandic when he came to pick up the faxes which had to do with detainees and exchanges. As far as Professor Koljevic is concerned, he wasn't on good terms either with Mr. Mandic or Mr. Stanisic. That's particularly true with regard to Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you able to say what was the reason Professor Koljevic was not on good terms with Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of it was of personal nature. However, Professor Koljevic always accused them of exceeding their authority, of wanting to wield more influence than what was proper. As far as Mr. Mandic is concerned, he regarded Mr. Koljevic with disdain, because Mr. Koljevic was a completely different personality to them. He was just a professor, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- were there -- were there any ways in which Professor Koljevic, specific ways in which Professor Koljevic regarded Mr. Mandic as not properly carrying out his functions as a member of the government?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in the work of the government, and I don't know that. Professor Koljevic attended government meetings on occasion. What he talked about on those occasions, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Professor Koljevic say anything to you about the relations between the members of the government and the group that I have mentioned just now, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and, well, himself, Professor Koljevic, and Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, Professor Koljevic and I, talked about either Mr. Mandic or Mr. Stanisic only when we started working together. Normally this was an informal conversation between the two of us where he would express his opinion of them. To put it simply, there were many things that he thought were not good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I did not get the impression from the first lines of the answer that the witness was answering your question. You were asked whether Professor Koljevic said anything about relations between the members of the government and the group just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, I'm grateful, Your Honour, Your Honour is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness starts answering a different question, then please take the witness again back to your question so that we get an answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Sorry, I was thinking that had been communicated to the witness. Mrs. Cenic, I had asked you whether Professor Koljevic had said anything to you about relations between, on the one hand, the members of the government, and on the other hand, that group that I mentioned, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic himself, and Plavsic. What is the answer to that specific question, please?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me about the government as a whole or are you asking me only about the people we mentioned, that's to say Mandic and Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I had quite deliberately said members of the government intending to embrace all the members of the government in that question, Mrs. Cenic, for clarification.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the government as a whole, we didn't discuss that. And I don't recall ever hearing Professor Koljevic discuss the government as a whole. His criticism was, as I said, leveled against these two persons, Mandic and Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, having put the question to you in that more general form and you've answered it, then did Professor Koljevic say anything to you about relations between on the one hand, Mr. Mandic, and on the other hand, that group, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the only answer I can give you to this question: As far as Mrs. Plavsic and Professor Koljevic are concerned, there was animosity between them, on the one hand, and Mr. Mandic, on the other. As far as Professor Koljevic's comments concerning Mr. Mandic and his relations with Karadzic are concerned, he thought that Mandic had far too much influence. As far as Mr. Krajisnik is concerned, to tell you the truth, we never discussed him or at least I don't remember. We never discussed the relations between Krajisnik, Stanisic, and Mandic, or between him and any other members of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Professor Koljevic say anything to you about the extent to which Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic were keeping Mr. Karadzic informed of their activities?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to you, Mrs. Cenic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'd like to come back to what you've said earlier, after your trip with this journalist, Mr. Kent. You stated [In English] "Which made it clear, at least to me, that the people were far from understanding the seriousness of the situation." [Interpretation] What did you mean by "[In English] "far from understanding"? [Interpretation] Could you please clarify that point, please? What do you mean by "the people"? Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to my work colleagues at the time, to the people I spent most of the time with, because they were at Pale in the offices there. They did not move about much, and were not in touch with reality, with what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for your employers, if I may use that phrase, as for your employers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that they didn't know either what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following: Did you react to all of this? Did you talk about it, not only to your colleagues at work, but did you also mention this to those you were working for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whoever wanted to hear what I had to say those days, I did. I did mention things, but I don't know whether I could have changed anything in the presence of the Croatian army. That is, the army of the Republic of Croatia. But whoever really listened or wanted to hear me out, whoever I sat down with, I would talk about my experiences from that trip. This was one of my confrontations with the reality and with what was happening to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was listening to you, I was very impressed by the words you used. You stated, among other things, about Derventa, that it was like a ghost town, and then you had that experience that was very difficult for you when you visited that detention centre. You stated that the atmosphere was very strange there. And through the words you used, I understood what you meant. So when you returned to Pale, didn't you go and see Mr. Krajisnik in order to tell him, "Things are going on, terrible things are going on"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that I went to him just for that purpose, that I talked to him about this particular thing. However, we did talk then and later on in informal conversations what was going on. Secondly, Mr. Krajisnik would often shake his head when I told him where I went and how I went there, and he was afraid for my safety. And as far as I'm concerned, it finally penetrated that the situation is even more terrible than we thought, and I tried to convey that message to everybody, and I also tried to tell them that this was not something that would be over, just like that, overnight, that nobody will say, "Okay, enough is enough, and let's put a stop to that." I still remember the images from that trip. They are very fresh in my memory, as something that was a turning point in my way of thinking also. I can't say with any degree of certainty whether my story had an impact on anybody, and what was done after that, what was the impression that I left with my story. Those were just the images that I conveyed. I don't know what the impression on people was and what was the result of my telling the story to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may I just mention, I hope it's not inappropriate, I've been informed that Mrs. Cenic is concerned about the length of time her evidence will take, but, Your Honour, I can offer, I hope, through the Trial Chamber this degree of reassurance that Mrs. Cenic's concern appears to be now that she might not finish her evidence before the weekend but, Your Honour, I'm so nearly finished that if we're having a normal day tomorrow, I hope, Your Honour, there doesn't seem to be any real chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Stewart, we will not have a normal day tomorrow because we will have a late start for urgent Tribunal matters. It was on my list to inform you about that, that we would start 45 minutes later tomorrow. I've got no idea, Mr. Harmon, do you have an impression on whether three hours -- not too many questions by the Judges, would --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can't calculate now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can't calculate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have to discuss that. Perhaps -- how many more minutes would you need, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can finish very quickly if Mr. Harmon operates within the guidelines we should finish tomorrow any way by my calculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 60 per cent of what is it now, four and a half hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I won't be more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, let's finish first. I'll do the calculations meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got just two documents with which the Court is very familiar, to put to the witness, and Your Honour would see I hope even if we haven't got a plethora of further photocopies of these documents it will be dealt with quickly. The first is P47 which I have in both the English and the Serbian. My copy can go on the ELMO, if necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness can look at it, I wouldn't say we know it by heart by now, but it's not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Quite -- here, Your Honour can have my copy by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just want you to take just a moment to familiarise yourself with that sufficiently, Mrs. Cenic, to say whether you recall seeing that document in 1992 or 1993. It's the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, and it sets out something called, in English, six strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you hear of the six strategic objectives when you were in Pale in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. That's that one, Your Honour. The other one I think an equally familiar document, although perhaps not known by heart is a document we have been using I think copy number 93, it's P529, it's also D10. It's something else in Mr. Trainer's exhibits as well, Your Honour. It's in loads of different places, but if I say we have been using number 93, Your Honour will know immediately what document it is -- well, Your Honours will know what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, talking about the A and B variant document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the previous one was P47, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This document, I'd like you to look at the Serbian version of this. There is an English translation but please look at the Serbian version. Again, just take enough time to familiarise yourself to answer the question, first of all, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you hear about variants A and B, or any similar name, in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Cenic. My last question, I think it will be. May I just put this to you, then, Mrs. Cenic? Your -- is it correct your father is a Serb, your mother is a Croat, and the -- one of the grandmothers or the grandfather and grandmother on one side of your daughter are a Muslim and a Croat?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My mother is a Croat. My father is a Serb. My uncle is a Hungarian. My mother-in-law comes from Boka. She is a Catholic, Croatian Catholic. People who reside in Boka are Catholics, Croats, and my father-in-law, Kemal Koraljic is a Muslim, Bosniak, although during his lifetime he declared himself as a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Perhaps the best way of proceeding is that we first discuss what will happen. Mr. Harmon, you said you were not yet in a position to calculate. I was. That is, the Defence took a little bit over five hours so three hours would be the 60 per cent. Even if we have a late start tomorrow, there should be three hours. If we have one break and if we would have a little bit long sessions, that is if we would start at 3.00, then continue until, well, let's say, 20 minutes to 5, and then have a break of half an hour, of course, with the support of the interpreters, so you're invited, I do not know whether there would be any additional questions, we would then not have time for re-examination so therefore you are invited while you went above the 60 per cent now and then, in one case even considerably, that's perhaps now to stay well within the 60 per cent, to see whether we can finish with the witness. Ms. Cenic, at the same time I have to inform you that although parties are now and then limited in the time they do not get all the time they would like to have, that it always also depends on how matters develop and whether we will be able to finish. We'll try to do our utmost best, Mr. Harmon and the Chamber and Mr. Stewart, but I can't promise you that we would finish tomorrow. At the same time, I do understand, because although the message was not addressed to the Chamber, Mr. Stewart, I got a courtesy copy of the information about the concerns of Mrs. Cenic, that if it would be necessary, that you would be willing to return, but, of course, we would like very much to save you the experience to have to go back and then to come back to the Tribunal again. Keeping this in mind, we would like to see you back tomorrow at 3.00 in this same courtroom. And I again instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony already given and still to be given. Would you please follow Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I observe, and I don't think it causes any problem at all to say this as the witness is leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what you are going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm saying I don't think it will, Your Honour. Your Honour, on behalf of the Defence I would submit unhappiness at the concept of re-examination being ruled out in advance on the basis there is no time with cross-examination taking place? Did I misunderstand what Your Honour was saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you misunderstand me. Because I said 60 per cent would be three hours, my calculation would be that we would have close to three and a half hours available, two long sessions, and I then invited, because I had exactly the same thoughts as you had, I invited Mr. Stewart to well remain within the three hours, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I see what Your Honour is saying. On a quick reading I thought Your Honour was saying something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially because then we would have just time -- for re-examination. Also added to that if need be we would ask the witness to come back. Then I was informed that you wanted to raise a matter about witnesses, and I have one matter on my agenda as well. If you could do that within two or three minutes I would need --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. It was simply to report the position to Your Honour. We now understand -- we have the next witness arriving this evening, God willing. He's on his way, we think. That's Mr. Kuzmanovic, no protective measures, clearly. He is arriving this evening. We are informed, I've been informed today, that Mr. Bjelica will be arriving here in The Hague on Monday. Your Honour, we are also bringing the next witness, whose name I won't then give Your Honour, we are bringing the next witness -- bringing her on Monday as well, Your Honour. Or possibly, I remember, Tuesday but whatever it is, Your Honour, we are bringing her in time for her to follow on Mr. Bjelica. It appeared to us that that was the mote suitable order of batting now, as far as witnesses can concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for updating us. I would like to inform the parties that on the 11th, that is not this Tuesday but next Tuesday that is the last day we would sit before we had a couple of days for further preparation of Mr. Krajisnik's evidence, that the Chamber had to decide that we'll sit in the afternoon rather than in the morning, as was scheduled, for urgent reasons. As far as the 20th of April is concerned, that would be the day when Mr. Krajisnik would start his testimony, the Chamber also had to decide that we would start in the afternoon and not in the morning which, of course, gives a couple of hours extra but so therefore these two days we will sit in the afternoon, not in the morning. Yes. Then finally, I would like to address you, Mr. Krajisnik, more directly because the Chamber wants to address various matters you have raised in Court on the 17th of March. I'm referring to transcript pages 21567 to 21571. One matter you raised, Mr. Krajisnik, is that the -- that many witnesses the Defence wished to call were too frightened to testify before this Tribunal. You referred to rumours that witnesses who have come to testify as Defence witnesses were punished or mistreated. The Chamber is concerned about these assertions. For the Chamber to be able to look into such incidents, however, the Defence would need to submit more specific information and is invited to do so. You also raised, Mr. Krajisnik, the issue of expert evidence. There has already been dealt with many times. The Chamber would only observe that by the 13th of January, 2006, the Defence no longer proposed calling political and history experts, focusing only on military and media experts. The Defence did not include any experts in its list of witnesses filed on the 7th of February and the 14th of February, and in its 14th of February response to the Chamber's priorisation - I'm now pronouncing it incorrectly - prioritisation order. Furthermore, as at the housekeeping session on the 23rd of February the Defence indicated at transcript pages 20853 to 854 that it had taken the decision not to call any expert witnesses. Considering what it takes for a party to prepare for an expert report and related testimony, the Chamber finds that it is not in the interests of justice at this stage to significantly prolong the proceedings so as to allow the Defence the time necessary to identify experts and present their reports. The Chamber notes that on the 28th of March, the Defence responding to a remark by the Chamber, asked whether expert evidence on the Defence side in relation to population movements would be of assistance. As we learned from expert witness Tabeau, there are many methodological issues with respect to statistical and demo a graphic studies. A great deal of work is required in order to obtain complete and reliable information. While such expert evidence is not indispensable to this case, the Chamber would consider a submission by the Defence to tender such evidence on the condition that the work has to a large extent already been completed and can easily be produced. The Chamber also understands that you have concerns regarding the amount of time available to the Defence, both for court preparation and actual time in court. With respect to preparation time, this Chamber has granted numerous extensions and recesses which we have documented in a series of decisions in order for the Defence to prepare for witnesses. For example, the Chamber granted the Defence an extra month to present its case as provided on the 27th of February. It has been left to the discretion of the Defence to allocate this time as it sees fit. So while you say that the main problem facing the Defence is time, we believe that the total time allotted for the conduct of your defence is adequate. As for the example you raised, Mr. Krajisnik, of witness Radojko. It is rather unusual the Prosecution cross-examined the witness one and a half times of the exam in chief. That is the example I just referred to, Mr. Harmon. Which is much longer than the 60 per cent guideline ordinarily followed in this case. In total, however, the Prosecution's cross-examination of Defence witnesses has lasted for approximately 64 per cent of time taken for examination-in-chief. In comparison, the Defence has's cross-examination of pros witnesses lasted for approximately 61 per cent of time taken for examination-in-chief. This difference is not negligible. However the Chamber suggests that cross-examination would take less time if, among other things, the Prosecution were provided with adequate witness information, well in advance of the schedule testimony. Given the limited amount of time remaining in the Defence case, the Chamber reiterates to the Defence the importance of providing meaningful notice of witness testimony. The Chamber will continue to regulate cross-examination so as to keep the Prosecution as close as possible to the 60 per cent guideline followed in this case. And that, Mr. Harmon, is valid for tomorrow. Also relating to witness Radojko, the Chamber is willing to consider favourably a motion for further re-examination due to the exceptional circumstances relating to this witness and the Chamber would request that such a motion specify the topics and the amount of time required for re-examination. On the 23rd of March, the Chamber granted the Defence several additional days in April which could be used for witness Bjelica and stated that it would provide further details in this response. We are well aware that we, the Judges, have spent during the Defence phase of the case, a greater proportion of testimony time on putting questions to witnesses, specifically. Whereas during the Prosecution phase our questions accounted for 8 per cent of the testimony time, during the Defence phase, to date, our questions have accounted for 19 per cent of that time. Performing the calculations you'll see that we have consumed an additional 15 hours of testimony time during the Defence phase so far, over and above what we would have consumed had we limited ourselves to the 8 per cent we used in the first phase. Of course, these proportions are not expected to remain exactly the same from one phase of the case to the other. Nevertheless we considered the difference in this instance large enough to justify the grant of three additional days to the Defence, namely the days of the 6th, the 7th and the 10th of April, with allowance made for testimony to spill over into a fourth additional day, namely the 11th, now reserved for outstanding procedural matters. I add to that at this moment that where I announced only seven minutes ago that we would sit in the afternoon of the 11th for urgent reasons that there seem to be practical problems in arranging for moving to the afternoon. We'll see how we will resolve that problem. One of the options being not having a complete morning session. The Defence will still have four court free days, namely the 12th, the 13th, the 18th and the 19th, to prepare for your testimony, Mr. Krajisnik, scheduled to begin on the 20th of April, as I said before, in the afternoon. Mr. Krajisnik, you also emphasised the importance of bringing in other witnesses in addition to giving evidence yourself. As we mentioned above, the Chamber has provided you adequate time to present your defence. The defence phase of the case must come to a close on the 6th of June. The Defence has identified the persons scheduled as the remaining witnesses in your case. We are also aware, of course, that we have allowed you to make changes to your expected schedule after seeking the Chamber's guidance. This Chamber is obliged to make findings based on the evidence heard, and it would be better able to do so with access to more information from persons who appear based on the evidence presented, to have had close contact with you during the relevant period or at least whether it would be close contact or at least people not far from you, to say it in general terms. Ignoring this information risks drawing wrong conclusions for or against either of the parties. As matters stand at this moment, this Chamber will decide at the close of the Defence case, whether to hear evidence from the additional witnesses we have in mind. Due to the logistical steps required in order to bring witnesses to the Tribunal, the Chamber will, however, start making arrangements already now for their possible testimony. Once the Chamber has finalised the procedure for the hearing of evidence from potential witnesses, we will identify these witnesses along with the procedure to enable the parties to conduct their own preparations. The Chamber will hear the parties' observations on the proposed procedure at the appropriate time. Lastly, Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber has not overlooked your remarks about your health and your living situation. You started with those observations. I will address them now at the end of this statement. As you may know, immediately following your statement in court, the Chamber had an OLAD representative contact Mr. McFadden of the detention unit and inform him of your remarks drawing attention to the change in your health condition. The Chamber has not been made aware of any further change in your health. We hope that your condition has improved. We trust that you will inform us if that is not the case. This concludes the statement on your remarks made on the 17th of March. Mr. Krajisnik, I see you raise your hand. We have limited time but if you would like to briefly say something, I would allow you to so with the permission of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be brief. I would kindly ask you to allow for a report to reach you on the movement of population. This can be done really very quickly. Secondly, thank you very much for your kind words. As I said at the beginning of this trial, when I asked for a lawyer, I was looking for a Dutchman and I found him here as a judge. You explain things so well that I cannot say anything but that I admire you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, thank you for this compliment. It's good to hear that at least you appreciate the efforts we are making to do our job as good as we can. As far as a report on the movement of population is concerned, Mr. Stewart, I again draw your attention to the difficulties, the methodological difficulties we also see already arising from the report of Ewa Tabeau. So therefore -- but if you can produce it, as I said, if it could be quickly produced, then we -- and if it's reliable data, if it's coping well with the materialogical problems involved then the claim would like to receive that as soon as possible. Mr. Krajisnik seems to be confident that it could be produced on short notice. I take it you'll discuss it with him and see whether you could present it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We will be discussing it, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Then we will adjourn, and I would like to again to thank the interpreters and the technicians. I know that I have got a bad reputation for now for their patience. We will adjourn to tomorrow afternoon at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 31st day of March 2006, at 3.00 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
